mods.title: Intro to R & RStudio
mods.excerpt: Created by statisticians for statisticians, R is the gold standard for data analysis. Understand the R ecosystem, RStudio IDE, and how to write your first script.
mods.body:
R is an open-source programming language and environment for statistical computing and graphics. It was created by Ross Ihaka and Robert Gentleman at the University of Auckland, New Zealand, in 1993. Today, R is the third-most popular language for data science, behind only Python and SQL.

Why Learn R?

  • Statistical Power: R was built by statisticians, for statisticians. It has the most comprehensive collection of statistical packages in the world.
  • Data Visualization: Libraries like ggplot2 produce publication-quality graphics with minimal code.
  • Reproducible Research: R Markdown allows you to weave narrative text and code together into dynamic reports.
  • Vibrant Community: CRAN (Comprehensive R Archive Network) hosts over 20,000 packages.

Your First R Script

R can be used interactively in the console or via saved scripts (.R files). RStudio is the recommended IDE. Let's write your first lines:

# This is a comment in R
# R uses the assignment operator <- (or =)
message <- "Hello, IT Study Hub!"
print(message)

# R is also a powerful calculator
2 + 3
sqrt(144)
pi * 4^2

# Getting help
?sqrt
help("mean")

Installing Packages

R's true power comes from its packages. The tidyverse is a collection of essential data science packages maintained by Posit (formerly RStudio).

# Install a package (run once)
install.packages("tidyverse")

# Load it into your session (run every time)
library(tidyverse)

mods.title: Variables & Data Types
mods.excerpt: R has unique data types designed for statistics. Master vectors, factors, lists, and understand the crucial concept of coercion in R.
mods.body:
R has five basic atomic data types: character, numeric (double), integer, logical, and complex. Unlike many languages, the most fundamental data structure in R is the vector — even a single number is a vector of length 1.

Creating Vectors

The c() function (combine/concatenate) is used to create vectors. All elements in an atomic vector must be of the same type.

# Numeric vector
ages <- c(20, 22, 19, 21, 23)

# Character vector
names <- c("Dithsha", "Mithila", "Rohan")

# Logical vector
passed <- c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)

# Integer vector (append L)
scores <- c(95L, 88L, 92L)

# Sequence generation
1:10
seq(0, 100, by = 10)
rep("A", times = 5)

Coercion Hierarchy

R automatically converts (coerces) elements to the most flexible type when mixed:

# logical → integer → numeric → character
c(1, "hello", TRUE)  # All become character
c(1, TRUE, 5)        # logical becomes numeric: c(1, 1, 5)

Factors — R's Statistical Superpower

Factors are used to store categorical data. They are internally stored as integers with associated labels (levels), making them memory-efficient and analysis-friendly.

gender <- factor(c("Male", "Female", "Female", "Male"))
levels(gender)       # "Female" "Male"
summary(gender)      # Counts per level

# Ordered factors
grade <- factor(c("B", "A", "C", "A"), 
                levels = c("F", "D", "C", "B", "A"),
                ordered = TRUE)

mods.title: Control Flow & Logic
mods.excerpt: Direct your data analysis workflow using conditional statements, loops, and R's powerful vectorized operations that eliminate the need for many loops.
mods.body:
Control flow in R follows standard programming paradigms, but R's vectorized nature means you often don't need explicit loops. Operating on entire vectors at once is both faster and more idiomatic in R.

Conditional Statements

score <- 85

if (score >= 90) {
  grade <- "A"
} else if (score >= 80) {
  grade <- "B"
} else if (score >= 70) {
  grade <- "C"
} else {
  grade <- "F"
}

# Vectorized ifelse (no loop needed!)
scores <- c(95, 82, 67, 91, 74)
grades <- ifelse(scores >= 90, "A",
          ifelse(scores >= 80, "B",
          ifelse(scores >= 70, "C", "F")))

Loops in R

While R supports for and while loops, they are generally slower than vectorized operations. Use them when vectorization isn't possible.

# For loop
for (i in 1:5) {
  print(paste("Iteration:", i))
}

# Looping over a vector
tech_stack <- c("R", "dplyr", "ggplot2")
for (tech in tech_stack) {
  print(tech)
}

# While loop
count <- 1
while (count <= 5) {
  print(count)
  count <- count + 1
}

The apply Family — R's Loop Replacement

R provides a family of functions to apply operations across data structures without explicit loops:

numbers <- list(a = 1:5, b = 6:10, c = 11:15)

# lapply returns a list
lapply(numbers, mean)

# sapply simplifies to a vector/matrix
sapply(numbers, mean)

# Apply to rows or columns of a matrix
mat <- matrix(1:9, nrow = 3)
apply(mat, 1, sum)   # Row sums (MARGIN = 1)
apply(mat, 2, mean)  # Column means (MARGIN = 2)

mods.title: Functions & Parameters
mods.excerpt: Break down analysis into reusable functions. Discover R's flexible argument handling, default values, and the powerful concept of lexical scoping.
mods.body:
Functions are the building blocks of reusable code in R. They encapsulate logic, accept inputs (arguments), and return outputs. R functions are first-class objects — they can be passed as arguments to other functions and returned from functions.

Creating Custom Functions

# Basic function
square <- function(x) {
  return(x^2)
}
square(5)  # 25

# Function with default arguments
greet <- function(name, greeting = "Hello") {
  paste(greeting, name, "!")
}
greet("Dithsha")           # "Hello Dithsha !"
greet("Mithila", "Hi")     # "Hi Mithila !"

# Multiple return values (as a list)
stats_summary <- function(x) {
  list(
    mean = mean(x),
    median = median(x),
    sd = sd(x)
  )
}
result <- stats_summary(c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5))
result$mean    # 3

The Ellipsis (...)

The ... argument allows a function to accept an arbitrary number of additional arguments, which it can then pass to another function.

my_plot <- function(x, y, ...) {
  plot(x, y, col = "blue", pch = 19, ...)
}

# Additional arguments like 'main' and 'xlab' are passed through
my_plot(1:10, 1:10, main = "My Chart", xlab = "X Axis")

Lexical Scoping

R uses lexical scoping, meaning functions look for variables first in their own body, then in the environment where they were defined.

outer_var <- 100

my_func <- function() {
  inner_var <- 50
  return(outer_var + inner_var)  # Can access outer_var
}

my_func()  # 150

mods.title: Data Frames & Tibbles
mods.excerpt: Data frames are the workhorse of R data analysis. Learn to create, index, filter, and manipulate tabular data — the foundation of all data science in R.
mods.body:
A data frame is R's most important data structure for data analysis. It is a two-dimensional table where each column can be a different data type (numeric, character, factor, etc.), similar to a spreadsheet or SQL table. Tibbles are the modern, enhanced version from the tidyverse.

Creating Data Frames

# Traditional data frame
students <- data.frame(
  name = c("Dithsha", "Mithila", "Rohan"),
  age = c(20, 21, 19),
  gpa = c(3.8, 3.9, 3.5),
  honors = c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE)
)

# Modern tibble (tidyverse)
library(tibble)
students_tib <- tibble(
  name = c("Dithsha", "Mithila", "Rohan"),
  age = c(20, 21, 19),
  gpa = c(3.8, 3.9, 3.5)
)

Indexing and Subsetting

R provides multiple ways to access data:

# By column name using $
students$age           # Returns vector: c(20, 21, 19)
students$gpa[1]       # First student's GPA: 3.8

# By position [row, column]
students[1, 2]        # Row 1, Column 2: 20
students[1, ]         # Entire first row
students[, "name"]    # Entire name column

# Logical subsetting
students[students$age > 19, ]   # Students older than 19
students[students$honors == TRUE, "name"]  # Names of honors students

Inspecting Data

head(students)        # First 6 rows
str(students)         # Structure of the object
summary(students)     # Statistical summary per column
dim(students)         # Dimensions: rows x columns
nrow(students)        # Number of rows
ncol(students)        # Number of columns

Why Tibbles?

Tibbles never convert strings to factors, never create row names, and print more cleanly. They are the default in the tidyverse and highly recommended for modern R workflows.

mods.title: Vectors, Lists & Matrices
mods.excerpt: Move beyond basic vectors. Discover matrices, arrays, and nested lists — the complete toolkit of R's core data structures for any analysis task.
mods.body:
While data frames handle most tabular data, understanding R's lower-level data structures is essential for advanced programming, linear algebra, and efficient memory usage.

Matrices — 2D Numeric Arrays

Matrices are two-dimensional structures where all elements must be the same type (usually numeric). They are essential for linear algebra and statistical modeling.

# Create a matrix
m <- matrix(1:9, nrow = 3, ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)
print(m)

#      [,1] [,2] [,3]
# [1,]    1    2    3
# [2,]    4    5    6
# [3,]    7    8    9

# Matrix operations
m * 2           # Scalar multiplication
t(m)            # Transpose
diag(m)         # Diagonal elements
det(m)          # Determinant
eigen(m)        # Eigenvalues and eigenvectors

Lists — R's Most Flexible Structure

Unlike vectors, lists can hold elements of different types and sizes, including other lists. They are the foundation for complex R objects like model outputs.

my_list <- list(
  name = "Dithsha",
  scores = c(95, 88, 92),
  matrix = matrix(1:4, nrow = 2),
  passed = TRUE
)

# Access elements
my_list$name        # By name
my_list[[2]]       # By position (returns the element)
my_list[2]         # By position (returns a sub-list)
my_list[["scores"]] # By name with double brackets

Combining Data

df1 <- data.frame(id = 1:3, score = c(85, 90, 78))
df2 <- data.frame(id = 1:3, grade = c("B", "A", "C"))

# Column bind
cbind(df1, df2$grade)

# Row bind
rbind(df1, data.frame(id = 4, score = 92))
